html:
The map's label for the farming peoples of the Ethiopian highlands, shown from 1500 BCE to the late 300s BCE in the south-west of the plateau. The highlands are cool and well watered, and their people developed crops found almost nowhere else.

What they grew:

  • teff, a tiny grain still used for injera bread;
  • finger millet and the oil seed noog;
  • enset, the "false banana", whose starchy stem feeds millions in the south;
  • wheat and barley brought from the Near East, ploughed with oxen.

Cattle, sheep and goats had come with herders from the north, part of the spread of herding into East Africa. Most people spoke Cushitic and Omotic languages.

In the north, around 800 BCE, the kingdom of Dʿmt arose with temples, such as the one at Yeha, and writing linked to southern Arabia, the root of the Ge'ez script. Its successor was Aksum. Little is known of the southern highland peoples in these centuries beyond what archaeology and language history suggest.
